name: secure-session-manager
intent: Centralise the creation, validation, renewal and invalidation of authenticated session state behind one manager and one store, so every request is checked against the same session policy and logout or privilege change revokes access immediately.
problem: Session state is handled ad hoc: identifiers come from weak randomness, sessions are created implicitly on anonymous requests, the identifier survives login unchanged, and logout clears only the client cookie, so revoked sessions stay usable and session fixation or hijacking defects surface only in review.
context: Web or API servers that keep authenticated state between stateless requests, where more than one instance may serve a user, where logout, timeout, password change or privilege elevation must take effect at once, and where the identifier travels in a cookie or header an attacker can observe, replay or fix.
benefits: One place decides session policy - identifier entropy, transport attributes, idle and absolute timeouts, regeneration triggers and invalidation rules - so audits and review have a single artefact to check.
Central invalidation: logout, password change, role change or administrative revocation delete the server-side record, and later requests carrying the old identifier fail closed.
The store abstraction lets the same policy run in-process for one instance and on a shared cache or database for a farm without touching call sites.
Identifier handling is separate from application state: the transported value stays an opaque reference, so no user data or privilege claim travels in the cookie.
Framework and language realizations share one vocabulary - create, validate, renew, invalidate - which turns the security review of a new service into a checklist over the same four operations.
tradeoffs: The session store becomes a shared failure domain and a per-request round trip: when it is unavailable every authenticated request fails although credentials are intact, and the hot path pays for a lookup.

The session identifier is a bearer credential; disclosure through the network, XSS, referrer headers or logs is full impersonation, so the pattern adds transport hardening (TLS, Secure, HttpOnly, SameSite, host-bound name) that must be kept up.

Stateless client-side variants (encrypted cookie, ticket) look cheaper but cannot be revoked: a copied cookie stays valid until expiry, so central invalidation forces a server-side record and with it the store dependency.
Coordination burden: server-side invalidation, client cookie clearing and cache directives are three separate acts, and an omission leaves a session usable after the user has seen a logout.
Distributed deployments reintroduce sticky sessions or a shared store, and identifier renewal windows create races where a legitimate request carrying the old identifier is rejected.
Timeout tuning is a security-usability tradeoff, and richer session data (impersonation flags, remember-me, cross-tab state) multiplies the renewal and invalidation paths that must be tested.

participants.responsibility: Single entry point that creates, validates, renews and invalidates sessions and is the only component that applies session policy.
Per-user state record: opaque identifier, authenticated principal, attributes, creation and last-use timestamps, idle and absolute expiry.
Backing persistence for session records (process memory, cache, database) shared by every instance that must validate the same identifier.
Produces unpredictable identifiers with a CSPRNG and sufficient entropy (OWASP: at least 64 bits, and 128 bits for a home-made identifier).
Carries the identifier over the wire (cookie or header) with Secure, HttpOnly and SameSite attributes, TLS-only delivery and a non-descriptive name.
Client of the manager: creates the session after successful authentication, triggers identifier renewal on privilege change and invalidates it on logout.

use_cases: Server-rendered web applications where a login must survive across requests and logout must revoke access immediately.
Stateless HTTP APIs that need authenticated continuity plus server-side revocation (administrative logout, device management, compromised-account response).
Multi-instance deployments behind a load balancer where any instance must validate the identifier, typically through Redis or a database-backed store.
High-value applications (banking, health, admin consoles) needing idle and absolute timeouts, regeneration on privilege change and reauthentication on risk events.
Single sign-on front doors that translate an external identity into a local session and terminate it independently of the identity provider.

Django sessions: SessionMiddleware owns the life cycle - django.contrib.auth.login() calls cycle_key() to mint a new session key while preserving data (fixation defence), logout() calls flush() to delete record and cookie, and SESSION_ENGINE plus SESSION_COOKIE_AGE/SECURE/HTTPONLY/SAMESITE concentrate the whole policy in settings.

Spring Session replaces the container HttpSession with a SessionRepository backed by Redis or a relational store so every instance validates the same identifier, while Spring Security's ChangeSessionIdAuthenticationStrategy rotates the identifier via HttpServletRequest.changeSessionId() at authentication.

ASP.NET Core session middleware: AddSession puts the record in an IDistributedCache backing store with a server-side IdleTimeout (default 20 minutes, reset per request), and the docs recommend a Redis/SQL distributed cache over sticky sessions in a web farm; express-session applies the same manager shape in Node - the cookie carries only the session ID while data stays in the store.
avoid_when: Machine-to-machine or service APIs with no human session: use short-lived scoped tokens or mTLS instead of a session store.
A single-page application served by a backend-for-frontend that already manages an HttpOnly cookie session: do not build a second session layer in the browser, and keep tokens out of localStorage.
Purely static or unauthenticated traffic: no session is needed, and creating one per anonymous request wastes storage and weakens privacy.
The framework defaults already satisfy the policy (Django, Rails, ASP.NET Core, Ktor, Vapor): configure timeouts and cookie attributes instead of replacing the mechanism.
anti_patterns: Hand-rolled identifier generation with a non-cryptographic RNG (timestamps, counters, UUIDv1, Math.random), which turns session hijacking into prediction.
Keeping the identifier unchanged across login (session fixation), or clearing only the client cookie on logout while the server-side record lives on.
Storing sensitive or authoritative data (balances, entitlements) in a client-side session cookie: it is replayable until expiry and signed data is often readable.
Making the session store the only copy of data that must survive restarts, or treating in-memory sessions as horizontally scalable.
Session identifiers in URLs, logs, analytics or referrer headers, and permissive cookie attributes (SameSite=None without Secure, wildcard Domain).
design_principles: Single responsibility and complete mediation: all session life-cycle decisions pass through the manager, and every request is validated rather than trusted.
Information hiding: application code sees an opaque identifier and a session object, never the store layout, expiry encoding or transport details.
Dependency inversion: policy depends on abstract store and transport interfaces, so in-process, cache and database backings are interchangeable.
Least privilege and fail-safe defaults: a session grants exactly its stored principal and scope, and any validation failure is treated as unauthenticated.
best_practices: Generate identifiers with the platform CSPRNG (OpenSSL RAND_bytes, crypto/rand, java.security.SecureRandom, secrets) and never reuse or shorten them.
Regenerate the identifier on every privilege change - login, role elevation, password change - and invalidate the old one immediately.
On logout invalidate the server-side record, clear the cookie and send cache directives (no-store, Clear-Site-Data) so browser caches do not retain session content.

Apply idle and absolute timeouts server-side; the client must not be the clock. OWASP suggests 2-5 minutes idle for high-value and 15-30 minutes for low-risk applications, with a 4-8 hour absolute limit.
Set Secure, HttpOnly, SameSite=Strict (or Lax) and a __Host- prefixed name on the session cookie, and keep the whole session on TLS.
Log session creation, renewal, invalidation and validation failures, correlating by a salted hash of the identifier instead of the identifier itself.
Bind the identifier to stable client properties (IP range, User-Agent, device) as an anomaly signal rather than a hard gate, and detect identifier brute force.
sources: Schumacher, Fernandez-Buglioni, Hybertson, Buschmann & Sommerlad, Security Patterns: Integrating Security and Systems Engineering (2005) - identity and session security patterns.
Nagappan & Steel, Core Security Patterns: Best Practices and Strategies for J2EE, Web Services, and Identity Management (2005) - Secure Session Manager for the web tier.
